props.title: Strike
props.initialSlug: Workers rise against brutal factory oppression

sections.content: Sergei Eisenstein's **Strike (1925)** (1925) revolutionized montage theory and working-class cinema. His debut feature showcases the innovative cross-cutting and intellectual montage that would later define Battleship Potemkin (1925) and **October** (1928). The film's depiction of a factory strike uses radical juxtaposition - cutting between workers and animals, machinery and violence - creating metaphorical connections that influenced everyone from Charlie Chaplin in Modern Times (1936) to Martin Scorsese's contemporary editing style.

sections.content: The film's influence on depicting labor struggles echoes through cinema history. Italian Neorealism drew directly from its documentary-like portrayal of workers, visible in **La Terra Trema** (1948) and **Bitter Rice** (1949). The tradition continues through Ken Loach's **I, Daniel Blake** (2016) and **Sorry We Missed You** (2019), maintaining Strike's unflinching look at working conditions.

Eisenstein's innovative visual metaphors - particularly the slaughterhouse sequence intercut with police violence - established a film language that directors still reference. **The Godfather** (1972) echoes this technique in its baptism montage, while **Apocalypse Now** (1979) employs similar cross-cutting to connect violence across different spaces. SUBHEAD: Soviet Montage Movement Impact

movies.title: Man With a Movie Camera
movies.slug: Dziga Vertov's experimental documentary showcasing Soviet montage theory

sections.content: While **Strike** emerged from the Soviet Montage movement alongside works like **The End of St. Petersburg** (1927) and **Earth** (1930), its technical innovations transcended political ideology. The rapid-cut sequences influenced Hollywood's approach to action and tension, visible in films from **Raging Bull** (1980) to **Black Swan** (2010). Eisenstein's theory of attractions - using shocking images to create emotional impact - remains fundamental to modern blockbuster cinema.
